issues.subcategory: results based on simulated data
issues.description: The manuscript presents inferential results and substantive conclusions even though the results were generated from a randomized dummy dataset rather than observed participant data. Randomly generated data cannot provide evidence for or against the hypotheses, cannot be used to evaluate replication success, and should not be interpreted as empirical findings.
issues.quote:
[IMPORTANT: 
Results were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.]

issues.subcategory: contradictory data-collection status
issues.description: The manuscript alternates between saying that data were simulated, that data collection was launched later, and that data collection was completed before analyses. These statements are mutually inconsistent and make it impossible to determine whether the reported analyses are preregistered results, simulated placeholders, or post-data analyses.
issues.quote: We first pre-registered the experiment on the Open Science Framework (OSF) and data collection was launched later that week. ... All measures, manipulations, exclusions conducted for this investigation are reported, all studies were pre-registered with power analyses reported in the supplementary, and data collection was completed before analyses.

issues.subcategory: hypothetical donation replaces real donation behavior
issues.description: The original dependent variable was an actual donation from an endowed $5 payment. The replication uses an imaginary donation intention from $0 to $5. Hypothetical willingness to donate is not equivalent to real costly prosocial behavior and is more vulnerable to social desirability, demand effects, and lack of incentive compatibility. This substantially changes the construct being measured.
issues.quote: Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.subcategory: removal of endowment procedure
issues.description: The replication removes the original procedure in which participants earned or received $5 before being asked to donate. This changes the psychological meaning of the donation decision: participants are no longer allocating windfall money or giving up real compensation. The absence of an endowment may alter generosity, perceived ownership, and loss aversion, making the replication non-equivalent.
issues.quote: No reward acquired from a pre-survey  Participants will not conduct an irrelevant survey prior to the experiment to earn $5 for the donation

issues.subcategory: merged original studies into one altered design
issues.description: Studies 1 and 3 in the target article tested different manipulations in separate experiments. The manuscript merges them into one 2 x 3 design and applies the explicit intervention to the joint condition, which did not occur in the original Study 3. This creates new cells and dependencies among comparisons, changes the meaning of the joint condition, and prevents a clean replication of either original study.
issues.quote: In this replication, we merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment to study both the explicit and implicit intervention of debiasing the identifiable victim effect... The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition to reveal a more comprehensive comparison between the explicit and implicit settings.

issues.subcategory: explicit and implicit manipulations confounded
issues.description: The design attempts to compare explicit and implicit debiasing, but the implicit condition is operationalized by adding victim statistics, while the explicit condition is a direct educational intervention. These manipulations differ in content, salience, demand characteristics, and target information, so differences cannot be attributed uniquely to explicit versus implicit deliberation.
issues.quote: For Hypothesis 3 and 4, explicitly learning about the identifiable victim effect means that participants would be presented with prior research about the phenomenon while participants implicitly learning about the effect would not be presented with such information but with the provision of victim statistics in the identifiable victim condition.

issues.subcategory: replication classified as close despite major deviations
issues.description: The manuscript classifies the study as a close to very close replication despite acknowledging different DV stimuli, different physical setting, different contextual variables, MTurk participants, hypothetical donations, and updated victim information. These are not minor deviations; several directly affect the core psychological process and outcome measure.
issues.quote: DV stimuli | Different | Question adjustment ... Imaginary donation ... Physical settings | Different | Online survey ... Contextual variables | Different | MTurk workers as participants ... Replication classification | close to very close replication

issues.subcategory: participant recruitment details missing
issues.description: Key information needed to evaluate the sample is missing, including geographic origin, recruitment criteria, MTurk eligibility filters, compensation, data-collection dates, exclusion rules, and whether participants were restricted to the United States. These details are especially important because charitable giving and reactions to African famine stimuli may vary by country, income, and cultural context.
issues.quote:
Geographic origin | US American | Not specified | Not specified
Gender | Not specified | 529 males, 471 females | 529 males, 471 females
... Compensation | US$5 | Not specified | Not specified

issues.subcategory: power analysis does not match design or hypotheses
issues.description: The power analysis is based on a two-group Cohen's d from the original intervention effect, but the replication uses a 2 x 3 factorial design, tests interactions, simple effects, post-hoc contrasts, correlations, and an extension outcome. Power for the focal interaction and planned simple-effect contrasts is not reported. The smallest original effect may also be inflated, and the manuscript does not power the study for the much smaller meta-analytic effect it cites.
issues.quote: To obtain the minimal sample size required for this study, a power analysis was conducted using Gpower with a power of 0.95 and an alpha of .05. Given the smallest effect size regarding the effect of intervention (learning identifiable victim effect or not) on donation was found in the original study with Cohens’d = -0.36, the corresponding sample size to detect such effect was 314.

issues.subcategory: omnibus ANOVA does not test stated hypotheses
issues.description: The main hypotheses concern specific comparisons: identifiable versus statistical victims, explicit debiasing for identifiable but not statistical victims, and implicit debiasing via the joint/statistics condition. The reported 2 x 3 ANOVA omnibus main effects and interaction do not directly test these hypotheses. In particular, a significant three-level identifiability main effect does not by itself establish the identifiable victim effect, especially when the interaction is significant.
issues.quote: We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on donation. Results from Table 9 showed that no significant effect was found on intervention but the identifiability and the interaction effect of identifiability and intervention was supported.

issues.subcategory: inappropriate planned contrast for interaction
issues.description: After finding an interaction, the manuscript compares the identifiable/no-intervention cell with the average of all other five cells. This contrast does not isolate the hypothesized explicit intervention effect among identifiable victims, nor the differential intervention effect between identifiable and statistical victims. Combining statistical, identifiable/intervention, joint/intervention, and joint/no-intervention cells into one comparison creates an uninterpretable contrast.
issues.quote: Given the significant interaction effect, we also conducted a t-test to study if the mean of  identifiable/no intervention condition is different from the mean of combining other five conditions on donation.

issues.subcategory: simple effects not reported for key hypotheses
issues.description: Hypothesis 3 requires testing whether the explicit intervention reduces donations in the identifiable condition but not in the statistical condition. Hypothesis 4 requires testing whether adding statistics reduces donations relative to the identifiable-only condition. The manuscript does not report these simple effects or interaction contrasts, so the key hypotheses are not actually evaluated.
issues.quote:
3 (Interaction effect) | Explicitly learning about the identifiable victim effect reduces donation to an identifiable victim but not to statistical victims
4 (Interaction effect) | Implicitly learning about the identifiable victim effect reduces donations to an identifiable victim

issues.subcategory: multiple testing not controlled across outcomes
issues.description: The manuscript tests multiple dependent variables and many effects: six segregated feelings, three effects for each, post-hoc tests, correlations across six conditions, and donation analyses. Only some pairwise comparisons use Bonferroni adjustment. The perceived-impact extension is declared significant at p = .045, but this would not survive correction for the family of segregated-feeling tests, making the conclusion likely overstated.
issues.quote: There was no significant result found on the main effect of intervention and the interaction effect on each affective feeling, only the result of identifiability on the perceived impact of donation yielded significant findings.

issues.subcategory: effect sizes inconsistent with test statistics
issues.description: The reported pairwise effect size for identifiable versus statistical victims is inconsistent with the means, standard deviations, t statistic, and sample size. A mean difference of about 0.30 on pooled SDs around 1.7 would imply a Cohen's d closer to 0.17–0.18, not 0.076. The confidence interval for d also includes zero despite a Bonferroni-significant p value, indicating either the effect size, CI, or p value is miscomputed or mislabeled.

issues.subcategory: perceived-impact post-hoc statistics inconsistent
issues.description: The perceived-impact post-hoc result reports t = 2.47 and Bonferroni-adjusted p = .041, but the reported effect size d = 0.08 is too small for the displayed mean difference and sample size, and the confidence interval includes zero despite the significant adjusted p value. This suggests a computational or labeling error.

issues.subcategory: sign of test statistic contradicts mean interpretation
issues.description: The t statistic for identifiable versus statistical victims is negative, but the text interprets the comparison as identifiable victims receiving higher donations than statistical victims. The sign may depend on contrast coding, but the manuscript does not define the coding, and the table label implies the opposite direction. This creates ambiguity about the direction of the effect.

issues.subcategory: original-study degrees of freedom inconsistent with N
issues.description: The manuscript reports Study 1 as N = 121 but gives denominator df = 115 for the 2 x 2 ANOVA. For a standard 2 x 2 between-subjects ANOVA with N = 121, the residual df would normally be 117. The discrepancy is not explained by exclusions, covariates, or missing data, raising concerns about the reconstructed original statistics.
issues.quote:
Effect of identifiability and intervention on donation (Study 1) (N=121)
... Identifiability |  |  | 1 | 115 | 6.75 | <.05* | .06

issues.subcategory: inappropriate use of Cohen's d for factorial interaction
issues.description: The manuscript reports the factorial interaction effect as Cohen's d. Cohen's d is not a natural effect-size metric for a two-way ANOVA interaction unless a specific contrast is defined. Reporting an interaction as d without specifying the contrast or conversion method is ambiguous and may misrepresent the original effect.
issues.quote: The interaction effect was d = 0.41, 95% CI [0.05, 0.77] when explicit learning was adopted to debias the identifiable victim effect.

issues.subcategory: bounded ordinal donation outcome modeled without justification
issues.description: Donation is a bounded $0–$5 response, likely discrete and non-normal. The manuscript uses ANOVA and Pearson correlations and explicitly drops the ordered probit model used in the original analyses, without checking assumptions or justifying why linear models are appropriate for a bounded ordinal/censored outcome.
issues.quote: Ordered probit regression | a. effect of identifiability on donation | This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.subcategory: practical significance ignored
issues.description: The manuscript describes the identifiability and interaction effects as supported despite extremely small partial eta-squared values. With N = 1000, trivial effects can become statistically significant, especially in simulated data. The manuscript does not compare the observed effect sizes with the original effects or evaluate whether the replication effect is meaningfully smaller.

issues.subcategory: post-donation feelings cannot predict donation causally
issues.description: The manuscript says correlations between feelings and donation test whether affective feelings predict donation, but feelings are measured after the donation decision. This temporal ordering makes reverse causation and post-hoc rationalization plausible. Correlations cannot establish that feelings caused or predicted donations.
issues.quote: After the donation, they had to fill up a questionnaire for different affective reactions they experienced which may influence their choice of donation.

issues.subcategory: correlational affect analyses framed causally
issues.description: The study aims to examine the effect of affective feelings on the identifiable victim effect, but affective feelings are not experimentally manipulated. Without manipulation, longitudinal ordering, or a preregistered mediation model with appropriate assumptions, the study cannot support causal claims about affective feelings influencing donations.
issues.quote: The second goal of the current research is to examine the effect of affective feelings on the studied phenomenon, with the introduction of an extension known as the perceived impact of donation.

issues.subcategory: explicit teaching not equivalent to deliberative thinking
issues.description: The central theoretical claim concerns deliberative or analytical thought, but the manipulation is teaching participants about the identifiable victim effect. Learning about a bias can induce demand characteristics, experimenter-demand compliance, skepticism, or moral correction; it is not a pure manipulation of deliberative reasoning.
issues.quote: participants under manipulation were taught about the identifiable victim effect before donating to the victims.

issues.subcategory: implicit learning construct mismatch
issues.description: The manuscript calls the joint/statistics condition implicit learning about the identifiable victim effect. However, participants are not learning the effect; they are receiving additional statistical information. This changes informational content and comparison context, so the manipulation does not validly operationalize implicit learning.
issues.quote: participants implicitly learning about the effect would not be presented with such information but with the provision of victim statistics in the identifiable victim condition.

issues.subcategory: identifiability confounded with number and vividness
issues.description: The identifiable and statistical conditions differ not only in identifiability but also in number of beneficiaries, narrative vividness, specificity, emotional detail, and likely perceived efficacy. Therefore, observed differences cannot be attributed solely to identifiability.
issues.quote: They received information either about the problem of starvation in Africa or a brief description of an African girl retrieved from the website of Save the Children as written on the charity request letter.

issues.subcategory: aggregated feelings scale lacks construct coherence
issues.description: The manuscript aggregates upset, touched, sympathy, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact. These are not all affective feelings; some are moral judgments or efficacy appraisals. Aggregating them without theoretical justification or psychometric evidence risks obscuring distinct mechanisms and producing an invalid composite.
issues.quote: Note: combine segregated feelings into one aggregated feeling

issues.subcategory: no reliability or scale validation reported
issues.description: The manuscript does not report item wording, response anchors, internal consistency, factor structure, or scoring rules for the aggregated-feelings measure. Without reliability and validity evidence, the reader cannot evaluate whether the composite meaningfully measures a single affective construct.
issues.quote: Segregated feelings include being upsetting, being touched, being sympathetic, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact of donation (extension)

issues.subcategory: perceived impact mislabeled as feeling
issues.description: Perceived impact is defined as perceived efficacy of one's contribution, which is a cognitive appraisal, not an affective reaction. Treating it as one of the segregated feelings and potentially aggregating it with emotions creates a construct mismatch.
issues.quote: Perceived impact refers to the perceived efficacy of contribution in expecting a favourable outcome (Erlandsson et al., 2015).

issues.subcategory: perceived-impact hypothesis conflicts with results and abstract
issues.description: The extension hypothesis predicts higher perceived impact for identifiable victims than statistical victims, but the abstract says lower perceived impact occurs for identifiable or joint conditions, and the results only show statistical victims higher than the joint condition. These statements do not align, and the reported result does not support the stated Hypothesis 6.
issues.quote: 6 (Extension) | An identifiable victim elicits higher perceived impact of donation than statistical victims

issues.subcategory: unsupported abstract conclusion for extension
issues.description: The abstract claims support for lower perceived impact when facing an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim with statistics, but the reported post-hoc test only finds a significant difference between statistical and joint conditions, not between identifiable and statistical conditions. The abstract overstates and changes the direction of the planned hypothesis.
issues.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.subcategory: no manipulation checks reported
issues.description: The study relies on participants reading and understanding the explicit intervention, the identifiable victim information, and the statistical information. No manipulation checks, comprehension checks, or attention checks are described. This is especially problematic for an online MTurk study where inattentive responding and bots are common concerns.
issues.quote: Participants will be assigned randomly to the intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.subcategory: procedure insufficiently described in manuscript
issues.description: The procedure section provides almost no procedural detail and directs readers to external supplementary materials and a Qualtrics link. A replicable manuscript should include the essential sequence, timing, exact manipulations, item wording or representative examples, scale anchors, randomization procedure, and exclusion/missing-data rules in the main text or stable supplement.
issues.quote: The session of “Procedure” in the supplementary summarizes the procedure of the current replication study. For the full reported survey, please access the Qualtrics survey with the link below: https://www.dropbox.com/sh/9sda2czfg6rzko3/AACsg1vIzXhMOInM7XMtV5ILa?dl=0

issues.subcategory: conditional and numerous analyses increase researcher degrees of freedom
issues.description: The analysis plan includes many outcomes, omnibus tests, conditional post-hoc tests, conditional contrasts, and correlations across six conditions. Although the study is described as preregistered, the manuscript does not clearly identify primary analyses or control the familywise error rate across all planned tests. Conditional testing rules leave substantial analytic flexibility.
issues.quote: Post-hoc contrast test   (Note: we conduct the test only if the interaction effect is significant)

issues.subcategory: original ordered-probit analysis omitted without justification
issues.description: The manuscript notes that the original study used ordered probit regression but states that the replication will not conduct it. Because the donation outcome is bounded and ordered, dropping this analysis could affect conclusions. The omission requires justification and should be specified as a preregistered deviation.
issues.quote: Ordered probit regression | a. effect of identifiability on donation | This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.subcategory: missing-data and attrition handling absent
issues.description: The manuscript says no samples were excluded, but it does not report incomplete responses, dropout after random assignment, failed attention/comprehension checks, duplicate MTurk IDs, bot screening, or how missing item-level data would be handled. For online experiments, these omissions threaten internal validity and reproducibility.
issues.quote: There was no exclusion of samples in this study.

issues.subcategory: online setting lacks control relative to lab original
issues.description: The original study was conducted in a controlled physical setting, whereas the replication is online. The manuscript acknowledges the change but does not address risks such as distraction, consultation with external sources, repeated participation, variable device displays, or reduced salience of the donation request.
issues.quote: Online survey Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study surveyed inside a student center of a university in Pennsylvania

issues.subcategory: overgeneralization to humans from unspecified sample
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly defines the effect as a general human tendency, but the proposed or simulated sample is MTurk-based, geographically unspecified, unusually old on average, and uses a specific charity/Africa context. The manuscript does not adequately limit claims to the sampled population or context.
issues.quote: The identifiable victim effect is a phenomenon characterized by the human’s tendency to give out more aid to a specific victim than to a group of statistical individuals.

issues.subcategory: implausible or unverified demographics
issues.description: The reported age distribution has a mean of 67.8, SD of 30.1, and range up to 120, which is unusual for MTurk and likely reflects the simulated dataset. If these were real data, they would require validation and screening; if simulated, they should not be reported as participant characteristics.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration (Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; 471 females and 529 males).

issues.subcategory: incomplete open-science links and preregistration review
issues.description: Several promised materials are missing or left as placeholders, and the OSF preregistration review field is blank. This undermines claims of full transparency and makes it harder to verify preregistration, peer review, materials, and deviations.
issues.quote:
Cloud folder for presentation (PPT and PDF) | <enter link here>
Cloud folder for peer reviews | <enter link here>

issues.subcategory: sample comparison table malformed
issues.description: The sample-comparison table appears to have duplicated replication columns despite only two column headers. This creates ambiguity about what values refer to the original study versus the replication and suggests reporting errors in basic study information.
issues.quote:
Table 4

Difference and similarities between the original study and replication

[TABLE]
 | Original study | Qualtrics generated response
Sample size | Study 1: 121 Study 3: 159 | 1000 | 1000

issues.subcategory: normative debiasing claim not justified
issues.description: The manuscript assumes that reducing donations to an identifiable victim is debiasing. However, whether equalizing donations by lowering aid to an identifiable victim is normatively better is not established. The manipulation may induce callousness rather than improved allocation, so the term debiasing requires justification.
issues.quote: The research conducted by Small et al. (2007) showed that the identifiable victim effect could be eliminated by deliberative thinking, meaning that thinking analytically about your helping behaviour would reduce your motivation to offer assistance to a single beneficiary.

issues.subcategory: analytical reasoning inferred from outcome suppression
issues.description: The manuscript treats reduced donation to identifiable victims as evidence that calculative or deliberative mechanisms were activated. Without direct measures of deliberation, cognitive reflection, reasoning process, or manipulation checks, the process inference is underidentified.
issues.quote: We aim to study the effect of deliberative thinking on identifiable victim effect by comparing the replication effect with the original effect

issues.subcategory: correlation analyses underpowered or uncorrected across six cells
issues.description: The manuscript conducts separate correlations between aggregated feelings and donation within six conditions, but does not adjust for six tests or justify the per-cell power. Null correlations are interpreted against the original study, but confidence intervals are wide enough to include nontrivial effects in several cells.
issues.quote: We conducted a correlation between aggregated feelings and donation to examine whether affective feelings predict donation. Results shown in Table 15 suggested that no significant correlation was found across all conditions

issues.subcategory: original-study statistics incompletely reconstructed
issues.description: The manuscript reports original p values only as thresholds, leaves several values as N/A, and does not provide enough detail on how original effect sizes and confidence intervals were computed. This limits evaluation of the replication comparison and may conceal discrepancies in reconstruction.
issues.quote: The effect size of the identifiable victim effect was not reported in the original study. Further calculation of the effect size and confidence interval was included in the supplementary under the section of “Power analysis of the original study effect”.

issues.subcategory: Study 3 denominator degrees of freedom omitted despite being computable
issues.description: The Study 3 one-way ANOVA has N = 159 and three groups, so the denominator degrees of freedom should generally be 156 unless exclusions or missing data occurred. Reporting df2 as N/A unnecessarily obscures the test and prevents verification of effect sizes.
issues.quote:
Effect of identifiability on donation (Study 3) (N=159)
... Identifiability Identifiable victim | 2.38 | N/A | 2 | N/A | 5.67 | <.01** | .07
